title: Install an underground system in an agricultural field

lessons.title: Planning and digging the trench
lessons.html:
What is an underground system?

On many farms, pipes are buried under the ground. They carry water from a pump, dam or borehole to irrigation lines, or they carry away extra water (drainage). Buried pipes are protected from sun, tractors and animals, and they do not get in the way of work in the field.

The plan

The farm manager or irrigation designer gives a layout plan. It shows where the main line and sub-mains go, the pipe sizes, where valves and hydrants must be, and how deep the trench must be. Follow the plan exactly. If something on the ground does not match the plan, stop and ask.

Before you dig

  • Find out where existing pipes, electric cables and telephone lines are. Hitting an electric cable can kill you.
  • Mark the line of the trench with pegs and string, or with lime.
  • Check that the pipes, fittings, glue and tools on site are the ones on the plan.

Digging the trench

  1. Dig by hand or with a trencher or TLB, as your supervisor decides.
  2. Dig to the depth on the plan. The pipe must be deep enough so ploughs and vehicles do not damage it.
  3. Keep the bottom of the trench smooth and even, with no sharp stones or roots that can damage the pipe.
  4. Keep the trench at the right slope (gradient) if it is a drainage line, so water flows the right way.
  5. Put the topsoil on one side and the subsoil on the other, so the topsoil can go back on top.

Trench safety

  • Deep trenches can collapse. Do not work in a deep trench alone and follow your supervisor's instructions on making the sides safe.
  • Keep spoil heaps and machines back from the edge.
  • Put up warning tape so nobody falls in, especially at night.
  • Wear safety boots, gloves and a hat in the sun.

lessons.title: Laying, joining, testing and backfilling
lessons.html:
Laying the pipe

Most underground pipes on farms are PVC or polyethylene (HDPE). Handle them carefully: do not drag them over stones or throw them off the bakkie. Keep the ends covered so soil and animals do not get inside.

  1. Put a layer of fine soil or sand at the bottom of the trench (bedding) if the plan asks for it.
  2. Lay the pipe in the middle of the trench, following the line.
  3. Leave the pipe a little snaking (not tight) so it can move when it gets hot and cold.

Joining PVC pipes

  • Cut the pipe square with a pipe cutter or fine saw. Remove burrs and clean the ends.
  • For glued joints, use the correct solvent cement. Apply it to both parts, push the pipe fully into the socket and hold it for a moment. Let it cure as the product says before putting pressure on it.
  • For rubber-ring joints, clean the ring, use the right lubricant and push the pipe in to the mark.
  • Polyethylene pipes are joined with compression fittings or welded by trained people.

Solvent cement is flammable and its fumes are harmful. Use it in fresh air, keep it away from flames and close the tin after use.

Valves and fittings

Install valves, tees, bends and hydrants where the plan shows. Put thrust blocks (concrete) at bends and ends if the plan asks for them, so water pressure does not push the pipe apart.

Testing

Before you fill the trench, the line is pressure tested. Fill it slowly with water to let air out, then bring it up to the test pressure given by the supervisor. Walk the line and look for leaks at every joint. Fix leaks and test again.

Backfilling

  1. Cover the pipe first with fine soil without stones, and press it down gently by hand or foot.
  2. Then fill the rest in layers, subsoil first and topsoil last.
  3. Leave valves and hydrants reachable and marked.

Record the pipe route, depth and valve positions on the farm map.

Key points

  • Follow the layout plan and find existing cables and pipes before digging.
  • Dig to the right depth with a smooth trench bottom.
  • Make clean, square cuts and correct joints.
  • Pressure test for leaks before backfilling.
  • Backfill with fine soil first and keep trench safety in mind.
